claim: The type V-A Cas12a protein can process its CRISPR array.
source: The type V-A Cas12a protein can process its CRISPR array, a feature useful for multiplexed gene editing and regulation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established capability of Cas12a.

claim: CRISPR arrays often exhibit unpredictable performance due to interference between multiple guide RNA (gRNAs).
source: However, CRISPR arrays often exhibit unpredictable performance due to interference between multiple guide RNA (gRNAs).
evidence: This is stated as a known problem in the abstract, supported by the experimental work in the manuscript.

claim: Cas12a array performance is hypersensitive to the GC content of gRNA spacers.
source: Here, we report that Cas12a array performance is hypersensitive to the GC content of gRNA spacers, as high-GC spacers can impair activity of the downstream gRNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: High-GC spacers can impair activity of the downstream gRNA.
source: Here, we report that Cas12a array performance is hypersensitive to the GC content of gRNA spacers, as high-GC spacers can impair activity of the downstream gRNA.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1G showing negative correlation between GC content and GFP activation.

claim: Natural repeats always contain an AT-rich fragment that separates gRNAs.
source: We analyze naturally occurring CRISPR arrays and observe that natural repeats always contain an AT-rich fragment that separates gRNAs, which we term a CRISPR separator.
evidence: This is based on analysis of 79 natural separator sequences from 30 bacterial species shown in Figure 2.

claim: Short, AT-rich synthetic separators (synSeparators) successfully remove the disruptive effects between gRNAs.
source: Inspired by this observation, we design short, AT-rich synthetic separators (synSeparators) that successfully remove the disruptive effects between gRNAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3D showing improved GFP activation with synSeparators.

claim: The synSeparator enables enhanced simultaneous activation of seven endogenous genes in human cells.
source: We further demonstrate enhanced simultaneous activation of seven endogenous genes in human cells using an array containing the synSeparator.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 5 showing improved activation of all seven target genes.

claim: Unlike Cas9, Cas12a can process its own CRISPR array without requiring tracrRNA and RNase III.
source: Unlike the widely used Cas9, which requires a trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) and RNase III for maturation of its gRNA, Cas12a (also known as Cpf1) can process its own CRISPR array (Fonfara et al., 2016; Zetsche et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CRISPR arrays encoding multiple crRNAs often exhibit unpredictable performance for multi-gene regulation.
source: However, CRISPR arrays encoding multiple crRNAs often exhibit unpredictable performance for multi-gene regulation.
evidence: This is stated as a known problem and motivation for the study.

claim: Array processing by Cas12a is uneven, such that constituent processed gRNAs may differ 10- to 100-fold in abundance.
source: Small-RNA-seq experiments suggest that array processing by Cas12a is uneven, such that the constituent processed gRNAs may differ 10- to 100-fold in abundance (Campa et al., 2019; Liao et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous small-RNA-seq studies.

claim: The full-length repeat sequence includes a short (~16–18 nt) fragment that gets excised and discarded during gRNA processing and maturation.
source: In their natural bacterial setting, the full-length repeat sequence includes a short (~16–18 nt) fragment that gets excised and discarded during gRNA processing and maturation, leaving the final, processed gRNA to consist of a post-processing repeat and a spacer (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The excised repeat fragment undergoes cleavage at its 3' end by Cas12a itself, and at its 5' end by an unknown bacterial enzyme.
source: The excised repeat fragment, which we here denote a CRISPR separator, undergoes cleavage at its 3' end by Cas12a itself, and at its 5' end by an unknown bacterial enzyme (Swarts, 2019; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Swarts, 2019 and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The separator has been omitted when Cas12a arrays have been experimentally expressed in eukaryotic cells.
source: For this reason, and because the separator has been seen as dispensable, the separator has been omitted when Cas12a arrays have been experimentally expressed in eukaryotic cells (Figure 1C; Campa et al., 2019; Kleinstiver et al., 2019; Tak et al., 2017; Zetsche et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: RNA secondary structure is known to impede Cas protein binding and processing.
source: RNA secondary structure is in fact known to impede Cas protein binding and processing in similar contexts.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Cas12a function is sensitive to hairpin formation downstream of the CRISPR array.
source: For example, Cas12a function is sensitive to hairpin formation downstream of the CRISPR array (Liao et al., 2019a), and gRNA processing is impaired by base-pairing of the repeat with regions outside the gRNA (Creutzburg et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: gRNA processing is impaired by base-pairing of the repeat with regions outside the gRNA.
source: For example, Cas12a function is sensitive to hairpin formation downstream of the CRISPR array (Liao et al., 2019a), and gRNA processing is impaired by base-pairing of the repeat with regions outside the gRNA (Creutzburg et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Creutzburg et al., 2020.

claim: Global RNA structure of the CRISPR array may negatively affect both gRNA processing and performance.
source: Global RNA structure of the CRISPR array may negatively affect both gRNA processing and performance (Liao et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liao et al., 2019b.

claim: The RNA-guided, RNA-cleaving protein Cas13 can be negatively affected by gRNA secondary structure.
source: Similarly, the RNA-guided, RNA-cleaving protein Cas13 can also be negatively affected by gRNA secondary structure (Abudayyeh et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: High GC content promotes RNA secondary structure formation because G-C base pairs contain three hydrogen bonds, compared to A-U's two hydrogen bonds.
source: One feature that promotes RNA secondary structure formation is high GC content (Chan et al., 2009) because G-C base pairs contain three hydrogen bonds, compared to A-U's two hydrogen bonds.
evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge and supported by citation.

claim: A single nucleotide change from T to G can lead to almost complete abrogation of GFP activation in extreme cases.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the CRISPR array sometimes displayed hypersensitivity to the composition of the dummy spacer: In extreme cases, a single nucleotide change from T to G led to almost complete abrogation of GFP activation in transfected cells (Figure 1F, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1F.

claim: There is a strong negative correlation between the GC content of the dummy spacer and GFP activation.
source: Intriguingly, we observed a strong negative correlation between the GC content of the dummy spacer and GFP activation (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; the percentage of GFP+ cells was a more sensitive measure of array performance than median GFP fluorescence, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1G with 51 CRISPR arrays.

claim: The percentage of GFP+ cells is a more sensitive measure of array performance than median GFP fluorescence.
source: Intriguingly, we observed a strong negative correlation between the GC content of the dummy spacer and GFP activation (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; the percentage of GFP+ cells was a more sensitive measure of array performance than median GFP fluorescence, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Permissive dummy spacers have relatively low GC content at the 3' end, close to the Cas12a cleavage site.
source: Interestingly, this analysis showed that 'permissive' dummy spacers had relatively low GC content at the 3' end, close to the Cas12a cleavage site.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H analyzing sliding window GC content.

claim: The GC content of the spacer's last few bases, close to the Cas12a cleavage site, is a more important determinant than the overall GC content of a spacer.
source: This suggested that the GC content of the spacer's last few bases, close to the Cas12a cleavage site, might be a more important determinant than the overall GC content of a spacer.
evidence: This is inferred from the sliding window analysis in Figure 1H-J.

claim: Knowing the average GC content of the last three nucleotides in the dummy spacer allows slightly better predictive power than knowing the GC content of the whole dummy spacer.
source: However, we found that simply knowing the average GC content of the last three nucleotides in the dummy spacer allowed slightly better predictive power than knowing the GC content of the whole dummy spacer (R2 = 0.52; Figure 1K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing R² values in Figure 1K.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between GC content and predicted secondary structure formation.
source: We indeed found a strong positive correlation between GC content and predicted secondary structure formation (R2 = 0.66; Figure 1L).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1L using RNAfold predictions.

claim: Spacer GC content is distributed around an average of 39%, with a range of 10–70% in naturally occurring Cas12a spacers.
source: However, we did not find any conspicuous absence of GC-rich spacers: Spacer GC content was distributed around an average of 39%, with a range of 10–70% (Figure 2A), though spacer GC content did vary between species and was weakly correlated with the overall genomic GC content (R2 = 0.16; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of 727 naturally occurring Cas12a spacers shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Spacer GC content is weakly correlated with the overall genomic GC content.
source: However, we did not find any conspicuous absence of GC-rich spacers: Spacer GC content was distributed around an average of 39%, with a range of 10–70% (Figure 2A), though spacer GC content did vary between species and was weakly correlated with the overall genomic GC content (R2 = 0.16; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Natural separator sequences show little sequence conservation except for a moderately conserved region at the very 5' end (GTYTA).
source: Overall, these separators showed little sequence conservation (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), except for a moderately conserved region at the very 5' end (GTYTA).
evidence: This is shown in the multiple sequence alignment in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a strong bias for low GC content in the 79 separator sequences analyzed.
source: However, we did detect a strong bias for low GC content in the 79 separator sequences (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B-C analyzing natural separators.

claim: Cas13d can process its own gRNA.
source: Like Cas12a, the type VI CRISPR RNA-cleaving enzyme Cas13d can also process its own gRNA (Konermann et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019), an ability that makes Cas13d attractive for multi-gene regulation on the RNA level (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Cas13d separators show a strong bias for low GC content, particularly at the 3' end of the separator, close to the Cas13d cleavage site.
source: We found a strong bias for low GC content here as well, particularly at the 3' end of the separator, close to the Cas13d cleavage site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C analyzing Cas13d separators.

claim: Sensitivity to spacer GC content is a factor that has shaped the evolution of multiple CRISPR-Cas systems.
source: This suggests that sensitivity to spacer GC content is a factor that has shaped the evolution of multiple CRISPR-Cas systems.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both Cas12a and Cas13d separators are AT-rich.

claim: Including the full 16-nt separator from L. bacterium almost completely abolished the array's function.
source: Including this separator, however, almost completely abolished the array's function, as almost no GFP activation was seen in the transfected cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3B.

claim: The long separator remains attached at the 3' end of each spacer because Cas12a cannot fully excise it.
source: One possible reason is that the long separator remains attached at the 3' end of each spacer because Cas12a cannot fully excise it (Zetsche et al., 2015; Zetsche et al., 2017), which might interfere with Cas12a function, as has been shown previously (Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: AT-rich synSeparators improve GFP activation compared with a single G nucleotide.
source: Interestingly, addition of an AT-rich synthetic separator improved the performance of the CRISPR array in all cases (Figure 3D), suggesting that a very short, AT-rich synthetic separator was sufficient to counteract the interference between gRNAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3D.

claim: The synSeparator exerts its main effect by facilitating gRNA insulation and processing rather than by adding a 3' AAAT extension to the GFP-targeting spacer.
source: We observed activated GFP expression with variant 2 but not with variant 3 (Figure 3F), supporting the hypothesis that the synSeparator exerts its main effect by facilitating gRNA insulation and processing.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing different separator positions in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Addition of the AT-rich natural separator or the synSeparator appears to loosen up secondary structures or create an accessible bulge at the Cas12a cleavage site.
source: Interestingly, addition of the AT-rich natural separator, or the synSeparator, appeared to loosen up these structures or create an accessible bulge at the Cas12a cleavage site (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is based on RNAfold secondary structure predictions shown in Figure 3H.

claim: CRISPR array performance is sensitive to both secondary structures limited to the dummy spacer and structures that involve the GFP-targeting gRNA's repeat region.
source: This indicated that CRISPR array performance is sensitive to both kinds of disruption.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B with designed secondary structures.

claim: The separator acts both by physically insulating gRNAs from each other and by breaking up secondary structures that involve two consecutive gRNAs.
source: We then included the AAAT synSeparator to these worst-performing arrays and found that this rescued CRISPRa performance in both cases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that the separator acts both by physically insulating gRNAs from each other and by breaking up secondary structures that involve two consecutive gRNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SynSeparators derived from other bacterial species can rescue poor GFP activation caused by a non-permissive dummy spacer.
source: Indeed, all these synSeparators improved performance of the GFP-targeting gRNA (Figure 3I), indicating that the effect was not sequence specific to the AAAT synSeparator.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3I testing multiple synSeparator sequences.

claim: Enhanced Cas12a from A. species (denAsCas12a) is also sensitive to spacer GC content.
source: Indeed, denAsCas12a was also sensitive to spacer GC content, and its performance was improved by the TTTT synSeparator (Figure 3J), indicating that sensitivity to spacer GC content is not limited to LbCas12a.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3J.

claim: No positional effect is observed from changing the spacer's position within a CRISPR array.
source: We observed no difference in GFP activation between any of the four arrays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). This indicates that position within a CRISPR array is not necessarily an important determinant of gRNA performance but may become important when the CRISPR array assumes tight secondary structures within a specific region as observed in Liao et al.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Array processing occurs both in the presence and absence of the synSeparator but is more efficient with the synSeparator.
source: The results showed that array processing occurred both in the presence and absence of the synSeparator but that it was more efficient with the synSeparator.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the in vitro cleavage assay shown in Figure 4B-E.

claim: At all time points, more single gRNAs had been processed from the array containing the synSeparator.
source: As Cas12a incubation proceeded for longer times, more single gRNAs were excised (41/42 nt and 45/46 nt in length without and with the AAAT synSeparator, respectively; Figure 4B,C; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for each point plotted separately), but at all time points more single gRNAs had been processed from the array containing the synSeparator (Figure 4E; see Materials and methods for calculations).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4E showing processing efficiency over time.

claim: The synSeparator improves Cas12a processing efficiency of CRISPR arrays.
source: Though the exact numbers may not correspond to what would be seen inside living cells, these results indicate that the synSeparator improves Cas12a processing efficiency of CRISPR arrays.
evidence: This is concluded from the in vitro cleavage assay results in Figure 4.

claim: Including the synSeparator increases activation levels of all target genes compared to the array without the synSeparator.
source: Including the synSeparator increased activation levels of all target genes compared to the array without the synSeparator (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 5B for seven endogenous genes.

claim: The improvement effect of the synSeparator varied from 1.1-fold to 8.0-fold but was consistent across all target genes.
source: The improvement effect varied, ranging from 1.1-fold to 8.0-fold, but was consistent across all target genes (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C comparing activation levels.

claim: The increase in gene activation with synSeparator is also seen on the protein level for GFP.
source: The increase was also seen on the protein level, which we could analyze for GFP via flow cytometry (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 5D measuring GFP fluorescence.

claim: Addition of a short, AT-rich sequence between gRNAs in a Cas12a CRISPR array can improve multi-gene activation in HEK293T cells.
source: These results indicate that addition of a short, AT-rich sequence between gRNAs in a Cas12a CRISPR array can improve multi-gene activation in HEK293T cells.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the endogenous gene activation experiments in Figure 5.

claim: High GC content at the 3' end of a spacer leads to poor performance of the downstream gRNA.
source: In this study, we found that Cas12a CRISPR arrays are sensitive to spacer GC content (Figure 1G). Specifically, high GC content at the 3' end of a spacer leads to poor performance of the downstream gRNA (Figure 1H–K).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1H-K showing the importance of 3' end GC content.

claim: Poor performance is likely caused by secondary structures that are either restricted to a single gRNA or involve two consecutive gRNAs.
source: This is likely caused by secondary structures (Figure 1M) that are either restricted to a single gRNA or involve two consecutive gRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by secondary structure predictions and experimental data.

claim: CRISPR arrays containing disruptive gRNAs are processed inefficiently by Cas12a.
source: CRISPR arrays containing such disruptive gRNAs are processed inefficiently by Cas12a (Figure 4B–E), which likely explains their poor performance.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the in vitro cleavage assay in Figure 4B-E.

claim: AT-rich separator sequences can break up secondary structures and give Cas12a access to its cleavage site.
source: However, AT-rich separator sequences, even short, 4-nt sequences, can break up such secondary structures and give Cas12a access to its cleavage site (Figure 3H), improving CRISPR array performance (Figure 3D–J).
evidence: This is supported by structure predictions in Figure 3H and experimental data in Figure 3D-J.

claim: Including short synSeparators between the gRNAs in a Cas12a array is a simple way to improve CRISPRa performance in human cells.
source: Consequently, including short synSeparators between the gRNAs in a Cas12a array is a simple way to improve CRISPRa performance in human cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This is the main practical conclusion of the study, demonstrated in Figure 5.

claim: The CRISPR separator found in natural Cas12a arrays acts as an insulator that reduces interference between adjacent gRNAs.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that the CRISPR separator found in natural Cas12a arrays acts as an insulator that reduces interference between adjacent gRNAs.
evidence: This is the main biological conclusion of the study based on all experimental data.

claim: The insulating effect of AT-rich CRISPR separators may be important enough to have helped shape the evolution of Cas12a CRISPR arrays.
source: This insulating effect of AT-rich CRISPR separators may be important enough to have helped shape the evolution of Cas12a CRISPR arrays.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that natural separators are consistently AT-rich.

claim: Design inspired by the natural CRISPR system can improve the efficacy of tools for CRISPR gene editing and regulation.
source: Furthermore, our study demonstrates how design inspired by the natural CRISPR system can improve the efficacy of tools for CRISPR gene editing and regulation.
evidence: This is the broader implication of the study's findings.

claim: Multiple crRNAs are encoded on a CRISPR array transcribed as a single, long transcript in their native prokaryotic context.
source: In their native prokaryotic context, multiple crRNAs are encoded on a CRISPR array transcribed as a single, long transcript (Brouns et al., 2008; Zetsche et al., 2015; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Multi-gene control can be achieved experimentally with Cas12a.
source: Therefore, multi-gene control can be achieved experimentally with Cas12a (McCarty et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McCarty et al., 2020.

claim: Cas12a arrays have been used to edit or control the expression of multiple genes in human cells.
source: This strategy has recently been used to edit or control the expression of multiple genes in human cells (Breinig et al., 2019; Campa et al., 2019; Kleinstiver et al., 2019; Tak et al., 2017; Zetsche et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The separator is not strictly needed for array function and has no known role.
source: The separator is not strictly needed for array function and has no known role, as far as we are aware.
evidence: This is stated as the prevailing understanding before this study.

claim: Cas12a cannot excise the separator on its own in mammalian cells, which means it remains attached to the 3' end of the upstream spacer.
source: Cas12a cannot excise the separator on its own, which means that it remains attached to the 3' end of the upstream spacer in mammalian cells (Zetsche et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zetsche et al., 2017.

claim: The fact that Cas12a arrays from all known bacterial species retain the CRISPR separator suggests that it might have a biological function.
source: Yet, despite being under intense evolutionary pressure, the fact that Cas12a arrays from all known bacterial species retain the CRISPR separator suggests that it might have a biological function.
evidence: This is inferred from the evolutionary conservation of the separator.

claim: The conserved region at the 5' end of the separator (GTYTA) possibly acts as a recognition motif for the unknown enzyme responsible for cleaving the separator at the 5' end.
source: This conserved region possibly acts as a recognition motif for the unknown enzyme responsible for cleaving the separator at the 5' end.
evidence: This is speculated based on the sequence conservation pattern.

claim: In natural CRISPR arrays, the separator aids CRISPR array processing by providing an AT-rich sequence that maximizes Cas12a accessibility to its cleavage site.
source: This opened the possibility that in natural CRISPR arrays, the separator aids CRISPR array processing by providing an AT-rich sequence that maximizes Cas12a accessibility to its cleavage site.
evidence: This is the hypothesis proposed based on the observation of AT-rich separators.

claim: The method developed can assemble CRISPR arrays containing up to 30 gRNAs.
source: To do this, we first developed a method for assembling CRISPR arrays using oligonucleotide hybridization and ligation, with which we could assemble CRISPR arrays containing up to 30 gRNAs (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as a technical achievement of the study.

claim: The 51 dummy spacer sequences were adapted from a negative-control sgRNA library generated by Gilbert et al., 2014.
source: The 51 dummy spacer sequences (Figure 1) were adapted from a negative-control sgRNA library generated by Gilbert et al., 2014.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: 727 naturally occurring Cas12a spacer sequences from 30 bacterial species were analyzed.
source: To address this question, we analyzed 727 naturally occurring Cas12a spacer sequences from 30 bacterial species containing the Type V-A CRISPR (Supplementary file 2; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as the dataset used for analyzing natural spacers.

claim: 79 unique separator sequences from 30 bacterial species were analyzed.
source: We analyzed 79 unique separator sequences from 30 bacterial species (Supplementary file 2; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as the dataset used for analyzing natural separators.

claim: The 6-nt CRISPR separator from 12 bacterial species containing Cas13d arrays was analyzed.
source: We similarly analyzed the 6-nt CRISPR separator from 12 bacterial species containing Cas13d arrays (Supplementary file 2; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as the dataset used for analyzing Cas13d separators.

claim: Poor performance of gRNAs containing the pre-processed Cas12a repeat downstream of the gRNA of interest has been reported previously.
source: This is consistent with a previous study that reported poor performance of gRNAs containing the pre-processed Cas12a repeat downstream of the gRNA of interest, which contains the separator (Liu et al., 2019), and is why previous designs have completely excluded any separator sequence.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Guide-RNA performance can be increased by adding RNA extensions to the 3' end of the gRNA's spacer.
source: Guide-RNA performance can be increased by adding RNA extensions to the 3' end of the gRNA's spacer (Creutzburg et al., 2020; Kocak et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The performance of Cas12a gRNAs starts to drop if RNA sequences > 13 nt long are attached to the 3' end of the spacer.
source: A recent study found that the performance of Cas12a gRNAs starts to drop if RNA sequences > 13 nt long are attached to the 3' end of the spacer (Nguyen et al., 2020), consistent with this hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nguyen et al., 2020.

claim: CRISPR-mediated multi-gene activation has been increasingly used for stem cell reprogramming and large-scale genetic screening.
source: Furthermore, because CRISPR-mediated multi-gene activation has been increasingly used for stem cell reprogramming and large-scale genetic screening (Replogle et al., 2020; Weltner et al., 2018), our method will further enhance these emerging applications.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.
